title: Disaster recovery and backups
subtitle: Pick an RPO and an RTO, keep backups that a bad script cannot reach, and time real restores until you know you can get your data back.

c.v: On 5 April 2022, a cleanup script at Atlassian deleted 883 sites. They belonged to 775 customers.
You met this outage in
incident response
, from the communication side. Here is the restore side.
Atlassian was not careless about backups. It kept them for 30 days. It could restore any data store to a chosen point in time. It also kept
immutable backups
and tested its restores.

The data did come back. For most customers, Atlassian restored to five minutes before the deletion. For 57 customers restored early, some databases first went back further, and Atlassian recovered the missing data later. It says no customer lost more than five minutes of data.
Time was the problem. The first customers got their sites back on 8 April. The last sites came back on 18 April. Some customers waited up to 14 days.

Why so slow? Atlassian regularly restored one customer or a small set of customers, and it could restore all customers into a new environment. It had no tested way to restore hundreds of sites into the live, shared environment. Each data store held data for many customers. So the team had to pull each deleted site out of the backups, piece by piece. With its first method, Atlassian estimated three weeks to restore everyone.
In its own words: "we missed our
RTO
but met our
RPO
Disaster recovery (DR) is your plan to get data and service back after something big goes wrong. That can be a lost data centre, a bad script, or ransomware.
Two numbers set the goal. The
RPO
(recovery point objective) is how much data, measured in time, you accept to lose. The
RTO
(recovery time objective) is how long you accept to be down. Atlassian describes them with two questions. How fresh is the data after you restore it? How quickly can you give it back to the customer?
Smaller numbers cost more. AWS calls the choice a trade-off between RTO and RPO on one side, and cost and complexity on the other. It also warns against a strategy that is stricter than you need.
You saw in the
replication lesson
that a
follower
copies every change from the
leader
. That includes a wrong DELETE, so a
replica
is not a backup. AWS says continuous replication "will not protect you against data corruption or destruction" unless you also have
point-in-time recovery
The key idea.
A backup counts only after you have restored it and timed the restore, at the size and shape of the disaster you fear. Until then, it is a hope.
Kinds of backup
A
full backup
copies everything. It is simple to restore, but big and slow.
An
incremental backup
holds only what changed since the previous backup. Since version 17, Postgres can take one with
pg_basebackup --incremental
. To restore it, you need it and every earlier backup it depends on. Postgres does not track that chain for you, so you must not delete a backup that a later one needs.
A
differential backup

holds everything that changed since the last full backup. To restore, you load the full backup, then only the newest differential. Differentials grow every day, so Microsoft suggests a new full backup at set times, for example weekly.
There is a second split. A
logical backup
, like
pg_dump
, writes rows as SQL. A physical backup copies the database's own files, or a disk snapshot of them. Postgres says logical dumps "do not contain enough information to be used by
WAL
replay".
So they cannot give you point-in-time recovery.
Point-in-time recovery
Point-in-time recovery (PITR) needs two things: a
base backup

of the data files, and an archive of every write-ahead log (WAL) file since then. To recover, you load the base backup and replay the WAL. You can stop the replay at any moment after the base backup ended.
Step through a recovery from a bad DELETE. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
You choose the stop point by time, by a named restore point, or by a
transaction
ID.
You need an unbroken chain of WAL files back to the base backup. One missing file breaks it. Postgres advises you to set up and test WAL archiving before you take your first base backup.
A physical PITR restores the whole database cluster, not one table or one customer.

Atlassian hit a similar problem at a much larger scale: its data stores were shared by many customers. Restoring one customer from a shared store means a restore to a side server, then a careful copy back.
Where the copies live
The
3-2-1 rule
says: keep 3 copies of important data (1 primary and 2 backups), on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite. A 2012 US-CERT paper states it and credits it to the second edition (2009) of
The DAM Book
, a book for photographers by Peter Krogh.
In the cloud, "offsite" should also mean "outside your
blast radius
". AWS says copying backups to another account helps against insider threats or a stolen account.
Attackers know where backups are. CISA says "many ransomware variants attempt to find and subsequently delete or encrypt accessible backups". It asks you to keep offline, encrypted backups.
An
immutable backup

cannot be changed or deleted until its retention time ends. CISA notes that some cloud vendors offer this, but says to use it "with caution". It may not meet some compliance rules, and a wrong setting can be costly.
Seatbelts against your own mistakes
Deletion protection.

Amazon RDS will not delete a database while deletion protection is on. It is on by default for databases created in the console. If you delete without keeping automated backups, RDS deletes those backups in the same region.
A
delayed replica
In Postgres,
recovery_min_apply_delay = '1h'
makes a standby apply each commit only an hour after the primary made it. That gives you time to stop it before a bad change arrives. Longer delays fill its disk with waiting WAL files.
Soft delete.
Mark data as deleted and remove it only later. After the outage, Atlassian committed to soft deletes, keeping deleted data until a retention period ends.
Test the restore, and time it

GitLab learned this in 2017. An engineer wiped the primary database while fixing replication, and the replica's data had already been wiped. The team restored from a disk snapshot made six hours earlier, which sat on a staging server. Copying it took around 18 hours, because the disks were throttled to about 60 Mbps.
GitLab also wrote that nobody owned the backups, so "nobody was responsible for testing this procedure".
AWS says your backup strategy "must include testing your backups", and suggests restoring on a schedule.
CISA also asks you to test backups "in a disaster recovery scenario".

A good restore test is a job, not a promise. Every week it restores the newest backup to a fresh server. It checks row counts and a few known records. It records how long the restore took, and it pages someone when any step fails.
A
game day
goes further. The team acts out a whole disaster, with people,
runbooks
and the clock running. After the outage, Atlassian committed to regular DR exercises that restore every product for a large set of sites at once.
AWS lists four strategies in order of rising cost and complexity, and falling RPO and RTO. The middle two,
pilot light
and
warm standby
, keep a second site partly ready. The ranges below are AWS's own.

head.v: What runs at the second site

c.v: Backup and restore
RPO in hours, RTO in 24 hours or less. PITR can bring RPO as low as 5 minutes in some cases.
Only backups. You rebuild servers and restore data after the disaster.
Most internal tools and young products. It is cheap and simple.
Pilot light
RPO in minutes, RTO in tens of minutes.
Data is replicated and always on. App servers are off until you need them.
Downtime of an hour hurts, but a second full stack is too costly.
Warm standby
RPO in seconds, RTO in minutes.
A smaller but working copy of the whole system. You scale it up.
Customer-facing systems where minutes matter.
Multi-site active/active
RPO near zero, RTO potentially zero.
Full production in every site, all taking traffic.
You already need several regions for users or law.
Simple rule:
every strategy still needs point-in-time backups. Even with
active/active
, a data disaster's recovery point "will always be at some point before the disaster was discovered".

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Ask the business for the RPO and RTO of each system, and write them down.
Ask,
"Which restore have we timed this quarter, and how long did it take?"
If nobody knows, the RTO is a guess.
List the disasters you plan for: a lost zone, a bad migration, a deleted customer, ransomware. Check that each one has a tested restore of the right shape.
Keep at least one backup copy in a separate account, with different credentials, that production scripts cannot delete.
Before a risky migration or bulk delete, take a fresh backup and know the restore time. See
schema migrations
Alert when a backup job fails or the newest backup is too old.
"Here is our Postgres setup. Write a weekly job that restores the newest base backup and WAL to a fresh server, runs these five checks, records the restore time, and fails loudly if any step fails."
"Read our Terraform. List every database, bucket and backup vault. For each, tell me if deletion protection, versioning or object lock is on, and who can delete it."
The restore test runs against a real, recent backup, not a tiny test database. Restore time grows with data size.
The checks look at data, not only at "the server started".
The backup credentials are different from the production credentials the agent saw. Code that can reach both is a
single point of failure
Retention is long enough to reach back past the time a bug could go unnoticed.

q.v: Your team has a Postgres primary and two replicas in other zones. Someone runs a DELETE with no WHERE clause. Why do the replicas not save you?

options.v: Replicas are read-only, so they cannot be promoted.
The replicas copy the DELETE too, a moment after the primary.
Replicas only keep the last hour of data.

why.v: Replication copies every change, good or bad. You need a backup that can go back to a moment before the mistake.

q.v: Your RPO is 15 minutes. You take one full backup every night and nothing else. What is wrong?

options.v: Nothing. A nightly backup meets any RPO.
A crash just before the next backup could lose almost a day of writes, far more than 15 minutes.
The RTO will be too short.

why.v: With only nightly backups, you can lose up to 24 hours of writes. Archiving the WAL for point-in-time recovery closes that gap.

q.v: Atlassian met its RPO in April 2022 but missed its RTO. What was the main reason?

options.v: Its backups were older than 30 days.
It had never tested its backups at all.
Its restore process was not built for restoring many sites out of shared data stores at once.

why.v: Atlassian regularly restored one customer or a small set, and could restore all customers into a new environment. It had no tested way to restore hundreds of sites into the live, shared environment.

q.v: Which DR strategy keeps data copied to a second site, but leaves the app servers there switched off until a disaster?

why.v: In a pilot light setup, the databases and storage are always on, but app servers are created or started only when you fail over.
